text: sp_recompile only forces the next call to compile a fresh plan. Whichever provider happens to run next becomes the new sniffed value, and the exact same problem returns for everyone else the moment a differently-sized provider calls it first. That's not a fix, it's the same bug on a delay.

The real fix is OPTION RECOMPILE, added directly to the statement. It tells SQL Server to compile a fresh plan for this specific statement, every single execution, using the actual parameter value passed in that time. No cached plan is ever reused across differently-shaped calls.

Compiling a fresh plan on every call costs real CPU, more than reusing a cached plan that happened to fit. That cost is worth paying here specifically because this procedure is called with wildly different appointment counts per provider — a handful versus hundreds — making one cached plan genuinely unreliable, not just occasionally suboptimal.

Validate across a small, a mid-size, and a large provider, timed in any order, repeated a few times. Before the fix, order mattered — whichever ran first set the pattern for everyone. After the fix, order no longer matters at all.

That independence from call order is the actual proof the fix worked, not just that one provider got faster. Next lesson wraps up everything built across this chapter — three real root causes, three real fixes, one healthier system.
